name: PT. Polychem Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Polychem Indonesia — a net-cash converter that is giving the land away
frontmatter.summary: Polychem runs one Merak site after closing polyester: a glycol train at a fifth of nameplate and an ethoxylate train at nine tenths. The operating business earns almost nothing. The balance sheet is the value, and the site is the option: the land sits on the books at 65.1 USD mm, more than four times what our DCF pays for the whole operating business. ADD, target Rp218 against Rp191.
thesis: The operating business is worth almost nothing and the DCF says so: gross margin of 1.1% in FY2025, 1.6% in FY2026E after a third-quarter gross loss, against SG&A of 2.5% of revenue, gives enterprise value of US$10.2m for two trains and a site [S2, S4, S5].

The reported turnaround is not operating: nine months of 2026 net profit of 4.4 USD mm sits on gross profit of 3.8 USD mm and 2.6 USD mm of other gains plus a 1.3 USD mm fair-value gain on the group's listed share portfolio [S4].
The balance sheet is most of the value: cash of 20.9 USD mm and no bank debt, plus a 8.9 USD mm listed portfolio, against a market capitalisation of IDR742.8bn [S4, S0].

The asset the market does not price is the land: 853,205 square metres under building rights across Merak, Karawang and Tangerang carried at 65.1 USD mm cost and never depreciated, against 36.2 USD mm of nine-month sales to the largest customer [S5, S4]. A sale or conversion of the site is the largest single value event available, and our bridge carries it at the bull probability.

The stock is a decision on the glycol train and the site, not a spread trade: a permanent shutdown, a conversion, a sale of the Merak or Karawang site or a trade remedy on petrochemical imports would each move the value more than the ethoxylate margin [S2, S10].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and the board's decision on the ethylene glycol train
Government decision on the industry association's safeguard and anti-dumping requests for petrochemicals
First-quarter 2027 financial statements, the first clean read on the post-polyester cost base
Annual general meeting: dividend resolution and auditor reappointment

blocks.text: **ADD, target Rp218, 14.1% expected total return.** PT Polychem Indonesia Tbk is a single-site petrochemical converter at Merak in Banten. It runs an ethylene glycol train and an ethylene oxide derivatives train, sells almost everything into Java, and has just permanently closed the polyester division that had been suspended since the pandemic and losing money for years [S2, S6]. The equity is backed by cash and a portfolio of listed shares, carries no bank debt, and trades at a fraction of its book value. The operating business earns essentially nothing, and the profit reported in 2026 comes from below the operating line [S4].

The variant view is about what is inside the book value and what the market is charging for it. A reader who screens on price-to-book sees 0.4x book and a net-cash balance sheet [S0, S4]. Most of that book is a glycol plant running at a small fraction of nameplate in an industry the government describes as oversupplied [S7, S8, S10], and we give the operating business almost no value. But the book also carries land: 853,205 square metres held under building rights in Merak, Karawang and Tangerang at 65.1 USD mm of cost, never depreciated [S5]. Our DCF pays US$10.2m for everything the company operates, so the land and the site are effectively free at today's price. The group has already closed one plant on this footprint, so a second decision of that kind is not a fantasy.

What the market is paying for, on our numbers, is the liquid balance sheet plus a going-concern value for the ethoxylate business and a fraction of the site. Our discounted cash flow puts enterprise value at US$10.2m and equity at Rp226 per share, against a price of Rp191 [S4, S0]. The probability-weighted target, after the house liquidity discount of 20.0% for a stock that trades IDR311.3m a day, is Rp218 [S0].

Three things move the value. First, a decision on the glycol train or the site: shutting it, converting it or selling the Merak or Karawang land would change the asset base more than any plausible movement in the ethoxylate spread, and it is worth more than a quarter of our target on a probability-weighted basis. Second, trade policy: the industry association has asked the government for safeguard and anti-dumping measures on petrochemical imports, and a favourable decision would lift domestic pricing across the product slate [S10]. Third, the group's use of its cash: the company holds a portfolio of listed shares in affiliated companies, and realising it, or a related-party transaction involving it, would be a governance event as much as a valuation one [S4].

The bear case is not a collapse; it is a slow grind. At a gross margin near zero the company covers its fixed costs only in good quarters, and the third quarter of 2026 was a gross loss [S4]. The bull case is a trade remedy plus a strategic decision on the site. Both are in the scenario table, and the base case is the most likely path: the ethoxylate train stays full, the glycol train keeps running at a low rate, and the company earns close to nothing for the foreseeable future. The rating rests on the site, not on the spread, and we say so rather than dress it up.

Polychem is one of the older names on the Jakarta exchange, listed in the early nineties as part of a group that also controls a tyre maker and a cable producer. Its history is the history of Indonesian upstream petrochemicals: a domestic industry built to supply the textile and packaging chain, then undercut by imported product as capacity elsewhere in Asia outgrew demand. Ethylene glycol is the antifreeze and polyester raw material; ethoxylates are the surfactants in detergents, personal care and industrial cleaning. Both are commodity chemicals sold on a spread over feedstock, and neither carries pricing power for a sub-scale producer.

Polychem operates one industrial site, at Merak in Banten, and reports one business segment, ethylene glycol and petrochemicals, after the polyester division was permanently discontinued [S4]. The site has two production trains. The ethylene glycol train has a nameplate capacity of 233,600 tonnes a year and produced 44,115 tonnes in FY2025. The ethylene oxide derivatives train, which makes ethoxylates and related surfactants, has a nameplate capacity of 80,000 tonnes and produced 71,941 tonnes in FY2025, about nine tenths of capacity [S2]. Total chemical sales volume was 100,617 tonnes in FY2025, down from the prior year as glycol output fell [S2].

The product slate is narrow. On the glycol side the company sells mono-, di- and tri-ethylene glycol and ethylene oxide. On the derivatives side it sells fatty alcohol ethoxylates, nonylphenol ethoxylates, tallow amine ethoxylates, castor oil and glycerine ethoxylates, plus two newer products, a cement grinding aid and a coolant [S2]. The company obtained halal certification for its glycol and ethoxylate products in November 2025, which matters for customers in personal care and food-adjacent applications [S2].

The polyester division is gone. Management suspended polyester operations in March 2022 because of the pandemic and the downstream market, and in November 2025 the board of commissioners approved a permanent discontinuation, disclosed to the exchange on 17 November 2025 [S6]. The stated reason was sustained losses, global oversupply, import competition and low utilisation; the company said there was no legal or financial impact because all obligations had been settled [S6]. The FY2025 accounts still carry depreciation of 4.1 USD mm, including the polyester share, and an impairment of polyester machinery was booked in the prior year [S5]. The annual report describes the decision in the same terms: the segment had lost money for several years and no longer contributed positively to the group [S2].

The customer base is concentrated and domestic. Sales to the three customers each above a tenth of net sales totalled 87.4 USD mm in the nine months to September 2026, roughly three fifths of revenue, and the largest single customer took about a quarter [S4]. Revenue by market was 137 USD mm in Java over the same period, with a small balance outside Java and in Asia [S4]. The company is therefore a supplier to Indonesian detergent, personal care and industrial customers, not an exporter; the annual report's export line is a rounding item [S5].

The supply side is more concentrated still. Raw materials used were 114 USD mm in the nine months to September 2026, of which purchases from PT Ecogreen Oleochemicals were 83.6 USD mm, the only supplier above a tenth of total purchases [S4]. Ecogreen is a palm-oleochemicals producer, and the relationship is the commercial core of the business: Polychem ethoxylates a palm-derived fatty alcohol feedstock and sells the surfactant, so its gross margin is the conversion spread on a feedstock it does not control and buys overwhelmingly from one counterparty [S4].

The company is controlled by three shareholders who hold 85.5% between them. Provestment Limited holds just under half the shares, PT Gajah Tunggal Tbk, the listed tyre maker, holds about a quarter, and PT Satya Mulia Gema Gemilang holds about a tenth [S2]. The general public holds the remaining 14.5%, which is above the exchange's free-float floor; the free-float figure in the data pack's registry mirror is inconsistent with the annual report's share register and we use the register [S2, F29]. The group relationship is visible in the accounts: Polychem sells steam and rents warehouse space to Gajah Tunggal, and it holds listed shares in Gajah Tunggal, KMI Wire and Cable, Equity Development Investment, Indonesia Prima Property and Bank Ganesha, all affiliated companies [S4]. The company employed 536 people at the last count [S0].

The Indonesian petrochemical industry is in a structural oversupply. A director at the Ministry of Industry said in November 2026 that China, which used to be an export destination for Indonesian feedstock, has built an integrated industry from upstream to downstream and now runs a surplus, and that producers in Russia, India, the United States and the Middle East have added capacity as well [S7]. Indonesia has two naphtha crackers against more in Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, so the domestic industry is sub-scale at the upstream end and dependent on imported feedstock [S7, S8]. The ministry puts installed polymer capacity at only part of domestic demand, yet imports still enter on price [S8].

Utilisation is the number that matters for a converter. The industry association told the ministry in November 2026 that member plant utilisation is running at a low level and asked for safeguard and anti-dumping measures, arguing that imports are being sold below normal value and that local producers cannot sell into their own market [S10]. The ministry has commissioned a review of dumping and of why utilisation is low, and is considering product standardisation as a second lever [S10]. For Polychem this is the central policy question: a safeguard or anti-dumping duty on the products it makes would raise the domestic reference price and could restore a spread; a review that ends without measures leaves the current competition in place.

The company's own market position is that of a small, non-integrated converter. It does not make ethylene; it buys a palm-derived feedstock and converts it. Its glycol train competes directly with imported mono-ethylene glycol from the large integrated producers in the region, and it has responded by running the plant down rather than fighting for share: glycol production fell to 44,115 tonnes in FY2025 while ethoxylate production rose to 71,941 tonnes [S2]. The annual report is explicit that the plan is to raise capacity utilisation in products with better margins, naming ethoxylate, and to reduce production of products that still contribute negatively, naming glycol [S2].

The moat is thin. The site has an integrated ethylene oxide unit, which is a genuine barrier to entry for a standalone ethoxylator because ethylene oxide is hazardous to transport and is normally consumed on site; that gives the Merak plant a defensible position in surfactants for Java-based customers [S2]. Halal certification and long relationships with the large detergent and personal care accounts add a little switching cost [S2, S4]. Against that, the company has no feedstock integration, one supplier for most of its raw material, three customers for most of its revenue, and no ability to set price in a market where imports set the floor [S4, S10].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is high: one oleochemical supplier provides most of the raw material and the company has no alternative at scale [S4]. Buyer power is high: three customers take about three fifths of revenue and can switch to imported surfactant [S4]. The threat of new entrants is low at the ethylene oxide stage, because of the capital and the hazard, but it is close to irrelevant, because the threat comes from imports rather than from new domestic capacity [S7, S10]. Substitutes are the petrochemical-based surfactants that compete with the palm-derived product, and their relative price moves with the oil and vegetable-oil complex. Rivalry is import-led and price-based, and the industry association's request for protection is an admission that domestic producers are not winning it [S10].

The external influences that matter are therefore three: the oil and palm complex, which sets the feedstock and the competing product's cost; trade policy, which sets the domestic price; and the rupiah, which affects the cost of imported inputs and the translation of dollar sales into local costs. The company reports in US dollars and sells in dollars, so the currency exposure sits in the cost base rather than the revenue line [S4, S5].

The house decks put numbers on the first of those, and the two series point in opposite directions. Brent runs from US$97.1/bbl spot to US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E and US$84.0/bbl in FY2027E, a fall of about an eighth, while the palm complex the feedstock actually keys off is forecast to rise: the CPO series runs US$1,135/t in FY2026E and US$1,240/t in FY2027E against US$1,007/t in FY2025A [S4]. The model links Brent because that is the reviewed energy series the chemicals template loads, and it exposes only the small Brent-linked slice of the cost base to it; the palm feedstock, which is the larger input, is carried through the revenue growth rate instead. We state the split rather than let the model imply the oil deck is the driver: a falling Brent path is a small margin positive for a converter that passes most of it on, and a rising palm path is the reason dollar revenue grows at all in FY2027E.

The history is a company that lost money through a downcycle and has only just stopped losing it. Revenue was US$142.8m in FY2022, fell to US$104.8m, recovered to US$109.7m and reached US$144.7m in FY2025 [S0, S5]. Gross profit went from a loss of US$-10m to a small positive of US$1.6m, a gross margin of 1.1% [S5]. Operating profit was negative in every one of those years, at US$-3.3m in FY2025, because SG&A of US$5.0m exceeded the gross profit [S5].

The 2026 interim accounts show the first genuine improvement in years, and also its limits. Nine-month revenue was 141 USD mm against a prior-year comparative of about three quarters of that, and gross profit was 3.8 USD mm, a gross margin of 1.6% on our full-year estimate [S4]. Raw materials used rose faster than revenue, by more than a third, which tells us the improvement is a pass-through of a higher feedstock price with a slightly wider conversion spread, not a volume story [S4]. SG&A was flat in dollars at 3.5 USD mm of general and administrative expense plus 0.2 USD mm of selling expense, so the operating result after those charges was close to zero [S4].

Below the operating line the picture is different, and this is the earnings-quality issue at the heart of the name. Nine months of 2026 produced net profit of 4.4 USD mm, but the operating result after SG&A was a small positive and the rest came from a 1.3 USD mm fair-value gain on the listed equity portfolio, a foreign-exchange gain and 2.6 USD mm of other gains [S4]. Those items are real cash in the sense that the portfolio can be sold, but they are not a run-rate, and we exclude them from the forecast [S4]. A reader who annualises the reported net profit will overstate the earning power of the business by a wide margin.

Our forecast follows the company's own plan and the last actual. FY2026E revenue is US$190.7m, a growth rate of 31.8%, because nine months are already booked and the fourth quarter is set at the third-quarter run-rate rather than at the strong second quarter [S4]. The half year made 4.5 USD mm of gross profit and the nine months made 3.8 USD mm, so the third quarter alone was a gross loss [S3, S4]. Applying that method to both revenue and cost gives FY2026E gross profit of US$3.0m and a gross margin of 1.6%, which is what the model carries: the input is calibrated so that the method and the printed number agree, rather than assuming the third-quarter loss reverses without evidence. FY2027E grows 4.0% and the later years 3.0% a year: the ethoxylate train is already at nine tenths of capacity, so there is no volume headroom, and the growth is the feedstock price carrying through plus modest demand [S2, S4]. The gross margin from FY2027E is held at the nine-month 2026 running rate, 2.6%: above the FY2025 actual because the polyester drag is gone and the mix is shifting to ethoxylate, and below the second-quarter 2026 spike because the third quarter was a gross loss and the industry is still oversupplied [S2, S4, S10].

Costs are the other half of the story. SG&A is essentially fixed in dollars, at about US$5.0m a year, so it falls as a share of revenue only slowly; we hold it at 2.5% of revenue [S4, S5]. Depreciation is the largest single charge in the business and the data pack gets it wrong: the pack carries US$4.1m for FY2025, which is only the general and administrative slice, while the accounts show 4.1 USD mm of depreciation in FY2025 and 4.7 USD mm in FY2024, most of it in manufacturing cost [S5]. We restate both years from the filing, and the restatement is what turns the reported EBITDA from a small negative into a small positive [S5].

The result is a company still below operating breakeven. Our FY2026E operating profit is US$-1.9m after a third-quarter gross loss that is carried into the fourth quarter, FY2027E US$-0.1m, and it only turns marginally positive from FY2028E as revenue grows against a fixed cost base [S4, S5]. EBITDA is US$2.3m, almost all of it depreciation. That is not a forecast of failure; it is what a zero-margin converter looks like, and it is consistent with the actual nine-month result. The FY2026E loss is a quarter worse than we printed before this revision because the fourth quarter now follows the third rather than the nine-month average.

Cash flow is better than the profit and loss, and this is where the house screens need care. Capital expenditure was 0.4 USD mm in FY2025 and less than that in the first nine months of 2026, against depreciation of 4.1 USD mm, so the plant is distributing its own depreciation rather than being renewed [S5, S4]. Operating cash flow was 10.1 USD mm in the nine months to September 2026 [S4], and it is not all structure: inventories fell from 24.4 USD mm at December to 17.7 USD mm in September, a release of roughly the difference, and the company also received a tax restitution and ran its payables up [S4, F39, F40]. Capex sits in investing cash flow and never enters that operating number, which is why the gap between capex and depreciation cannot explain it. Working capital is close to neutral rather than a call on cash: net working capital was US$2.7m at the last year end and a small positive balance in September 2026, because the supplier funds the inventory [S4]. We model working capital at 1.0% of revenue, the September position [S4].

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the company. At 30 September 2026 total equity was 117 USD mm, cash was 20.9 USD mm, and there was no bank debt: total liabilities of about two fifths of that equity figure are trade payables, accruals, contract liabilities, taxes and an employment-benefit obligation, with only a small lease liability that resembles borrowing [S4]. The company also holds 8.9 USD mm of listed equity securities, which the data pack folds into its cash line; we carry the whole liquid balance inside net debt rather than count it twice, but we mark the portfolio down and say why in the valuation section, because it is invested in five affiliated small caps that the same group controls [S4, S0]. Against that, the company carries 154 USD mm of accumulated losses, which is why it pays almost no tax and why there is no distributable reserve to pay a dividend from [S4].

Capital allocation has been conservative to the point of inertia. There is no dividend and none is proposed, the annual general meeting in June 2026 resolved against one for FY2025 because the year was a loss, and the cash has accumulated rather than been deployed [S9, S4]. The one deployment the company has made is the listed equity portfolio, which is invested in affiliated companies rather than in the business [S4]. That is a governance question as much as a capital-allocation one, and we return to it in section six.

Earnings quality, run through the house screens and stated the way the card asks for it. The accruals ratio is (net profit less operating cash flow) over average total assets. In FY2025 the company made a net loss of US$-3.1m while operating cash flow was 3.2 USD mm on average total assets of about 153 USD mm [S5, F33, F34], so the ratio is negative — cash earnings exceed accounting earnings, and the same is true of FY2023 and FY2024, when the losses were far larger and cash burn smaller [S0]. A negative accruals ratio is the conservative direction and is not our flag. The genuine flag is the composition of profit: nine months of 2026 net profit of 4.4 USD mm rests on 2.6 USD mm of other gains and a 1.3 USD mm fair-value gain, not on the spread [S4], and none of that is forecast.

The divergence flags need the calendar as well as the arithmetic. Trade receivables jumped from 10.5 USD mm at 31 December 2025 to 26.9 USD mm at 30 June 2026, which is more than one and a half times revenue growth and would trip the card on its own [S3, S4, F35, F42]; but by 30 September they were back to 16.4 USD mm [S4, F41], so the spike is a half-year peak, not a deteriorating collection cycle. We still say DSO roughly doubled at the June date and that a repeat at the December close would be a flag. Inventories fell through the period and the margin improved, which is the opposite of an inventory build. On the exchange regime screens we found no special notation, no material legal case and no administrative sanction disclosed for last year [S2]. The public holds 14.5% of the shares, above the exchange's free-float floor, so there is no liquidity-driven index event in the base case [S2, F29]; what remains is a thin float that we handle through the target discount rather than as a listing risk.

We value Polychem on a discounted cash flow of the operating business, with the liquid balance sheet added at face value. The method fits because the multiples do not: EBITDA is almost entirely depreciation, so an EV/EBITDA multiple is really a multiple of the accounting charge, and the price-earnings multiple is meaningless when net profit is a fair-value gain one year and a loss the next [S4, S5]. The company is a finite-life converter whose plant is being run down, so the cash flow that matters is the depreciation it distributes before the asset needs replacing.

The discount rate is the house build for an Indonesian basic-materials name. The risk-free rate is 4.9%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the country risk premium 2.5%, and the industry unlevered beta 0.90 relevered for a company with no net debt, giving a cost of equity of 10.9% and a weighted average cost of capital of 10.9% [S4]. The cost of debt is irrelevant at this leverage. We do not add a company-specific premium to the discount rate; the small size, the customer and supplier concentration and the thin free float are handled in the scenarios and in the separate liquidity discount, not hidden inside the WACC.

The DCF produces enterprise value of US$10.2m and equity value of Rp226 per share. The shape of the result is the point. Free cash flow is about US$2.4m in the explicit forecast because capital expenditure runs far below depreciation, and it falls to almost nothing once the plant must be renewed at the depreciation rate [S5, S4]. The terminal value is 0.0% of enterprise value, which is why the answer barely moves with the terminal growth rate or with a percentage point on the WACC: the value is the cash the plant throws off before it has to be replaced, plus the net cash.

The capex profile is not a convention, it is the asset life. At 31 December 2025 net property, plant and equipment was 92.8 USD mm, of which 65.1 USD mm was land carried at cost and never depreciated, leaving the depreciable base against a FY2025 charge of 4.1 USD mm: an average remaining depreciable life of about seven years, with machinery alone at a similar multiple of its own charge [S5, F7, F31, F36]. We therefore ramp capex from 0.4% of revenue to 1.0% and 1.8% and settle at the depreciation rate from FY2031E, which is when the remaining life of the two trains runs out and replacement can no longer be deferred. A shorter life would take the explicit-period value down and a longer one would take it up; the point is that the step is dated by the filing's own depreciation arithmetic, not by the fifth year of a spreadsheet.

Two items sit outside the DCF and both are in the bridge. The first is the site. The group owns 853,205 square metres of land under building rights in Merak, Karawang and Tangerang, carried at 65.1 USD mm of cost and never depreciated, with the rights running to dates between 2027 and 2046 [S5]. The DCF pays US$10.2m for the operating business that sits on it, so a sale or conversion of the site is worth the land less the operating value given up. We carry that net amount at the bull probability, because a sale is a decision the controlling group has not announced and the precedent is the polyester closure rather than a property transaction [S2, S6]. The second is the listed portfolio: 8.9 USD mm of shares in Gajah Tunggal, KMI Wire and Cable, Equity Development Investment, Indonesia Prima Property and Bank Ganesha, all affiliated [S4]. We mark it at a discount rather than at par, because a company with a 14.5% public float holding five low-float affiliates cannot realise quoted prices at size and the group decides both when and to whom they are sold. The 1.3 USD mm fair-value gain booked in the nine months is already inside the carrying value, so the mark is not stale; the discount is about realisability, not about the mark.

The cross-checks are informative precisely because they disagree. On EV/EBITDA the stock is at 4.2x our FY2027E EBITDA, which looks cheap until you notice that the EBITDA is depreciation [S5]. On price-to-book it is at 0.4x book, which looks cheaper still until you ask what the book is: a glycol plant at a fifth of nameplate and an ethoxylate plant at nine tenths, in an industry the government calls oversupplied [S2, S7]. A price-to-book method that marks the company at book value produces a value several times the market price, and we have deliberately given it no weight: it would be a liquidation value for assets that cannot be liquidated at book, and the company is not being liquidated. The free-cash-flow-to-equity yield of 0.1% is the cross-check we take most seriously, because it is the cash an owner actually receives, and it is consistent with the DCF [S4]. It is also the number that shows why the equity is not a bond: the yield is high only because the market price is low relative to a cash flow that stops when the plant needs replacing.

The sensitivity grid is unusually flat, and that is a finding rather than a defect. Because the terminal value is negligible, a percentage point on the WACC or on terminal growth moves the value by a few rupiah, not tens of rupiah. What moves the value is the gross margin and the length of time the plant can run without replacement capital: a percentage point of gross margin is worth more than a percentage point of discount rate, which is why the scenario table, not the WACC table, is where the risk sits.

What the price implies. We do not run a reverse DCF here, because the value does not respond monotonically to the driver the engine can invert: with capex settling at the depreciation rate, a higher revenue path adds almost no free cash flow, so an implied growth rate would be a number without a meaning. The decomposition is more honest. At Rp191 the market is paying less than our base value of Rp251 and well below the bull, and the gap between the price and the base is roughly the site option we carry in the bridge [S4, S5]. In other words the market is paying for the operating business and the cash, and is charging us nothing for the land. That is the variant view, and it is the one thing in this valuation that a decision by the controlling group can crystallise.

The scenario values frame the range. Our base case is Rp251, the bear case Rp132 and the bull case Rp455, weighted at the probabilities in the table below and then cut by the liquidity discount to the Rp218 target [S4, S10]. The asymmetry is real and it comes from the operating leverage of a zero-margin business: a small improvement in the spread is worth a great deal, and a small deterioration takes the operating value to zero, at which point the equity is worth the net cash.
The downside risks, with our assessment of likelihood and impact.

**Commodity and spread risk (high likelihood, high impact).** The company's gross margin is a conversion spread of a couple of percentage points, and the feedstock is a palm-derived oleochemical bought mostly from one supplier [S4]. A move in the palm or oil complex that the company cannot pass through within a quarter takes the margin to zero; the third quarter of 2026, with Brent near its high for the year, was a gross loss [S4, S6]. This is the risk that drives the bear case.

**Trade policy (medium likelihood, high impact, two-sided).** The industry association has asked for safeguard and anti-dumping measures, and the ministry has commissioned a review [S10]. A favourable decision would raise domestic prices and is the main bull-case driver. An unfavourable one, or a slow one, leaves the import competition in place. The risk is two-sided but the timing is not in the company's hands.

**Operational concentration (medium likelihood, medium impact).** One site, two trains, one of them running at a low rate and the other at nine tenths of capacity [S2]. An unplanned outage on the ethoxylate train would remove most of the gross profit; the company carries insurance but the earnings are not diversified. The glycol train is old enough that the company impaired machinery in the prior year [S5].

**Customer concentration (medium likelihood, high impact).** The three customers above a tenth of sales took 87.4 USD mm of the 141 USD mm booked in the nine months to September 2026, and the largest alone took 36.2 USD mm, a quarter of revenue [S4, F24, F32, F9]. Size it in earnings rather than in adjectives: at our base gross margin the largest account carries roughly a third of the group's gross profit, so losing it would take the operating business from marginally profitable to loss-making before any replacement volume, and the customer is a domestic consumer-goods group that can buy the same surfactant from an importer [S4, S10]. We do not model the loss because there is no evidence of a change in the relationship and the account grew year on year [S4], but it is the single largest operating risk after the spread itself, and it justifies the wide bear.

**Supplier concentration (medium likelihood, high impact).** PT Ecogreen Oleochemicals supplied 83.6 USD mm of the 114 USD mm of raw materials used in the nine months to September 2026, roughly three fifths of cost of goods sold and the only supplier above a tenth of purchases [S4, F11, F12]. This is a bigger exposure than the customer side, because there is no second source at scale for a palm-derived fatty alcohol of that specification and the ethylene oxide unit is integrated to that feedstock. A change in Ecogreen's allocation or pricing policy would hit the spread directly, and unlike a lost customer it could not be replaced from imports on the same terms. It is also the reason we treat the palm complex, not Brent, as the real cost driver [S4].

**Governance and related parties (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The three holders above five per cent own 85.5% of the shares between them and the public holds 14.5%, which is above the exchange's free-float floor but thin [S2, F29, F37]. The company holds a portfolio of listed shares in affiliated companies, and it transacts with its tyre-making shareholder for steam and warehousing [S4]. None of this is improper on the evidence we have, but it means minority holders depend on the controlling group's decisions about cash, and a related-party transaction is the most likely route by which value is transferred. The registry figures in the data pack are internally inconsistent with the annual report's register, which is why we use the register [S2].

**Liquidity (high likelihood, medium impact).** The stock trades IDR311.3m a day and the public holds 14.5% of the shares [S0, S2]. We apply the house liquidity discount of 20.0% to the target, and an investor who needs to exit a position quickly will do worse than the screen price.

**Currency (low likelihood, low impact).** The company reports and sells in dollars, so translation is not the issue; the exposure is in rupiah-denominated costs against dollar revenue, which is a modest tailwind when the rupiah weakens [S4, S5].

The bear case is the third quarter's gross loss made permanent. Revenue growth runs four points below base in every year and the gross margin is a little over a point lower, which puts the spread back at the FY2024-FY2025 level of about one per cent, the trough the audited accounts actually printed rather than a hypothetical one [S5]. The company still has the net cash, so the equity does not go to zero; it goes to the value of the liquid balance sheet plus a small operating value, which is why the bear falls to Rp132 and not to nil.

The bull case is a trade remedy plus a spread a little over a point wide of base, which puts it just under four per cent: above the nine-month 2026 average and below the second-quarter spike [S4, S10]. Revenue growth runs four points above base, the site is worth more than its running value to a strategic buyer, and the listed portfolio is realised with the proceeds available to minorities. The operating value rises sharply because the fixed cost base does not move, which is what takes the bull to Rp455.

The shocks are mirrored at four points of growth and about one and a third points of margin in each direction, and the probabilities reflect the evidence: base is the most likely path at half the weight, the bear is a real possibility at a quarter given the third-quarter gross loss, and the bull is a quarter because it depends on a policy decision we cannot date [S10]. The base case is not the cautious case; it is the method the company itself is running, and it still leaves the site unvalued.

The signposts that would change our view, in order of importance: a board decision to shut, convert or sell the glycol train; a safeguard or anti-dumping duty on the products the company makes; a change in the ethoxylate spread sustained over two quarters; a related-party transaction involving the listed equity portfolio; and any change in the public float, a tender offer or a capital reduction [S2, S4, S10].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. Provestment Limited holds just under half the shares, PT Gajah Tunggal Tbk about a quarter and PT Satya Mulia Gemilang a tenth, 85.5% between them, and the general public holds 14.5% [S2, F37, F29]. We take the share register from the annual report rather than the registry mirror in the data pack, because the mirror's own rows do not add to a hundred per cent and the report's do [S2]. The public holding is above the exchange's free-float floor, so there is no listing or index consequence to argue about; the float is simply thin, at IDR311.3m of turnover a day [S0]. The company is not on the exchange's special monitoring list and we found no enforcement action, no index deletion and no group transaction requiring disclosure in the registry we checked [S0]. The practical consequence of the ownership is that minority holders have little influence over capital allocation, and the cash on the balance sheet is controlled by the group.

The board is small and the same names recur. The president director is Gautama Hartarto, the vice-president director is Djali Halim, and the board includes Gunawan Halim, Djunali Djuwati and Wiji Santoso; the president commissioner is Bacelius Ruru, and there are three further commissioners, two of them independent [S9]. The annual general meeting in June 2026 was attended by shareholders representing the large majority of the shares, re-appointed the directors and commissioners, and approved the prior year's accounts [S9]. The auditor is the Indonesian member firm of Deloitte, which issued an unqualified opinion on the most recent audited accounts [S5, S9]. We found no auditor change, no qualification and no restatement in the period we reviewed.

Related-party dealings are small in the trading line and larger on the balance sheet. Sales to the affiliated tyre maker and its subsidiary are a rounding item, and the company receives steam and rental income from Gajah Tunggal that runs to a fraction of a million dollars a year [S4]. The larger exposure is the 8.9 USD mm listed equity portfolio, which is invested in Gajah Tunggal, KMI Wire and Cable, Equity Development Investment, Indonesia Prima Property and Bank Ganesha, all affiliated companies [S4]. That is a real asset at market value, and we count it in net cash, but it is also a related-party concentration and a use of cash that does not fund the business.

The dividend record is empty and the reason is structural, not a policy preference. No dividend has been paid in the period the data pack covers, and the 2026 annual meeting resolved against a dividend for the prior year because it was a loss [S0, S9]. With 154 USD mm of unappropriated accumulated losses at 30 September 2026 the company has no distributable profit from which a cash dividend could be paid: Indonesian company law allows a distribution only out of positive retained earnings, and the shareholders in general meeting decide the appropriation [S4]. The deficit has to be absorbed first, and the only two routes are future profits, which at the modelled earning rate would take a very long time, or a deficit or capital reduction approved by shareholders, which carries creditor-notice and solvency requirements. Neither is announced in any filing or resolution we have seen [S9].

That matters to the rating in both directions. It is why the base case pays nothing and why the cash sits in the valuation as net cash rather than as a dividend stream, and it is also why the cash-return route is a bull-case leg rather than a base-case one: a controlling group that wants the cash out can clear the deficit and distribute, and the market is not pricing that option. We flag the route and do not model it, because modelling a corporate action nobody has announced is how a base case stops being the most likely path [S9, S4].

On ESG, the exposures are those of a coastal petrochemical site: process emissions, water discharge into the Merak coastal area, and the safety of ethylene oxide handling, which is the reason the site is integrated rather than tolling [S2]. The company obtained halal certification for its main products in 2025, which is a product-quality and market-access matter rather than an environmental one [S2]. We found no disclosed environmental sanction or material legal case in the annual report [S2]. The governance score is held back less by any single finding than by the combination of a thin free float, a controlling group, a cash pile invested in affiliates and a board that has not changed in the period we reviewed.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The nearest is the government's response to the industry association's request for safeguard and anti-dumping measures, which the ministry said in November 2026 it would study [S10]. The next is the full-year audited results, expected in the first quarter of 2027, which will be the first complete year without the polyester division and the first clean read on the post-closure cost base [S2, S4]. The annual general meeting follows in the second quarter, with the dividend resolution and the auditor appointment [S9]. The first-quarter 2027 accounts will show whether the fourth-quarter 2026 spread held.

The KPIs we monitor between updates are these. First, the ethoxylate production rate against the nameplate: at nine tenths of capacity there is no volume upside, so any fall is a demand signal [S2]. Second, the glycol production rate against the nameplate: the number itself matters less than the direction, because a decision to stop is the single largest value event available to the company [S2]. Third, the gross margin, which is the whole operating model and which we track quarterly because it swung from a strong second quarter to a gross loss in the third [S4]. Fourth, the spread between raw material purchases and revenue, which tells us whether the pass-through is holding [S4]. Fifth, the cash balance and the listed equity portfolio, which together are most of the equity value [S4]. Sixth, any related-party transaction, any change in the free float, and any trade-policy decision affecting petrochemical imports [S4, S10].

What would make us wrong on the upside: a trade remedy that lifts the domestic price across the slate, a decision to convert or sell the glycol train, or a sustained widening of the ethoxylation spread that turns the operating business into a genuine earner [S2, S10]. What would make us wrong on the downside: a spread collapse that takes the operating value to zero, a loss of the largest customer, or a related-party use of the cash that minority holders do not share in [S4]. We would revisit the rating on any of these, and on the publication of the audited full-year accounts.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +31.8%: nine months of 2026 are already booked at USD 140.84m against USD 106.27m a year earlier (+32.5%) [S4, F9], and the fourth quarter is set at the third-quarter run-rate in both revenue and cost (Q3 alone was USD 49.84m of revenue after USD 91.01m at the half [S3, S4]), giving USD 190.7m for the year. The driver was feedstock pass-through plus capacity fill, not demand: raw materials used rose 35.1% to USD 113.79m over the same nine months [S4, F11] while the ethoxylate train is already at 90% of its 80,000 t capacity (71,941 t produced in FY2025) [S2, F6], so there is no volume headroom left for FY2027E. FY2027E +4.0% is the palm-linked feedstock (61% of COGS) carrying through at roughly the 2026 rate less the house Brent path: the deck runs Brent from 96.0 in FY2026E to 84.0 in FY2027E, and on the 5% of COGS that is Brent-linked and 90% passed through [S4] that shaves about half a point off dollar revenue, so the gross growth is a little above 4%. FY2028E-FY2030E +3.0% a year is Indonesian chemicals demand growth once the capacity fill is done, and the terminal rate 2.0% is below the explicit years, not above them.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The margin is the ethoxylation spread and it is thin. Nine months of 2026 printed 2.67% (gross profit USD 3.76m on USD 140.84m of sales) [S4, F10], against 1.13% for FY2025 and 0.94% for FY2024 [S5, F2, F4]. FY2026E is set so that the FULL YEAR reproduces the stated method - nine months booked plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate: Q3 alone was a gross LOSS of USD 0.745m (USD 3.760m at nine months less USD 4.505m at the half [S3, S4]), so the full year comes out at about 1.6% and that is what the input is calibrated to at FY2025 input prices (the link below adds about 0.2pp of cost). We do not assume the third-quarter loss reverses: there is no disclosure of a Q4 recovery in the Q3 LK signed 29 October 2026 [S4]. From FY2027E we hold an effective 2.4%, the running rate implied by the nine-month average rather than by the Q3 trough: above the 2022-2025 trough of about 0.5%, because the loss-making polyester division is gone [S2, S6] and management is shifting capacity from glycol, which it says still contributes negatively, to ethoxylate, which it says carries better margins [S2], and below the Q2 2026 spike, because national petrochemical utilisation is only 60%-70% on dumped imports and the industry association is asking for trade remedies, not reporting a demand recovery [S10, S7].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Raw materials are 83% of cost of goods sold (USD 113.79m of USD 137.08m in the nine months to September 2026) and the largest single input by a wide margin is the palm-derived feedstock bought from PT Ecogreen Oleochemicals, USD 83.58m or 61% of COGS [S4, F11, F12]. That feedstock keys off the palm/CPO complex through biodiesel, not off crude one-for-one, so the Brent-linked share is the non-Ecogreen raw material at 22% of COGS [S4, F11, F12] further cut for the ethylene feed that only the glycol train consumes at a fifth of nameplate [S2, F21]: we apply 5% of COGS, not 20%, and the 2026 evidence supports a small number because raw materials rose 35.1% while revenue rose 32.5% and the gross margin still improved, so pass-through is close to complete [S4, F9, F11]. Net of the 90% pass-through that is 0.5% of COGS exposed, and the report states the modelled Brent effect from that figure.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set at 90%. This is a converter with a 2%-3% gross margin: it quotes customers a formula price and the feedstock moves through within a quarter, which is why 2026 revenue rose 32.5% with raw materials up 35.1% and the spread barely moved [S4, F9, F11]. The 10% residual is the working-capital and timing leak. With link1_share at 5% the net exposure is half a per cent of COGS (5% x 10%), so the house Brent path from 96.0 in FY2026E to 84.0 in FY2027E moves gross profit by about 0.07% of COGS - around three per cent of the modelled gross profit, not enough on its own to swing the rating [S4].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Selling plus general and administrative expenses were USD 3.61m in the nine months to September 2026 (USD 0.16m selling, USD 3.45m G&A), 2.56% of revenue, and USD 4.97m for FY2025, 3.44% [S4, S5, F14]. The cost is essentially fixed in dollars (salaries USD 2.23m and employment benefits USD 0.45m of the G&A line [S4]), so we hold 2.6% on the higher 2026 revenue base rather than let the ratio drift as revenue moves.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: depreciation was USD 4.117m in FY2025 and USD 4.660m in FY2024, of which USD 3.879m ran through manufacturing cost and USD 0.011m through G&A in FY2025 [S5, F7, F8], against the data pack's USD 0.011m, which is only the G&A slice of the charge. Nine months of 2026 depreciation was USD 3.093m [S4], an annual rate of about 4.1m. Against the 2026 revenue base of USD 190.7m that is 2.2% and the charge is falling only slowly because capex (USD 0.41m in FY2025 [S5, F13]) is far below depreciation: the Merak plant is being sweated, not renewed.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capital expenditure was USD 0.41m, 0.3% of revenue, and nine months of 2026 USD 0.19m [S5, F13, S4]; the group sold USD 1.09m of property, plant and equipment in the same nine months, so it is shrinking its asset base, not building it [S4]. The plant is being sweated, and the filing dates the end of that: at 31 December 2025 net depreciable assets (PP&E net of the un-depreciated land) were USD 27.7m against a FY2025 depreciation charge of USD 4.117m [S5, F7, F31, F36], an average remaining depreciable life of about seven years, with machinery net of USD 17.8m against a machinery charge of USD 2.6m. We therefore ramp capex from 0.4% of revenue to 1.0% and 1.8% across FY2029E and FY2030E and settle at the D&A rate from FY2031E [S5], which is when the remaining depreciable life of the two trains runs out and replacement can no longer be deferred; a perpetuity growing 2.0% a year cannot be funded by capex running below depreciation.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: At 30 September 2026 trade receivables of USD 16.41m plus inventories of USD 17.66m less trade payables of USD 32.84m gave net working capital of USD 1.23m, 0.87% of nine-month revenue [S4]: the supplier funds the business, with payables roughly double receivables. We set 1.0% of revenue, the September position, rather than the 1.9% the data pack shows for FY2025, because the payable balance is the structural feature and inventory has been run down from USD 24.37m at December to USD 17.66m [S4].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The group carries USD 154.2m of unappropriated accumulated losses at 30 September 2026 [S4, F17]. Nine months of 2026 paid USD 0.18m of tax on USD 4.63m of pre-tax profit, 3.9%, and FY2025 booked a net benefit [S4, S5]. That 3.9% is charged on pre-tax profit which at the operating line was close to zero, so the paid rate is already the after-shield rate and not a precursor to a ramp: the shield is 154.2m against pre-tax profit of the order of one million a year, and most of that pre-tax profit is interest income rather than the spread. The most-likely card requires the rate the LK shows being paid, so we hold 4%, the measured nine-month rate, through the forecast and in the terminal year, rather than ramp to the 22% statutory rate on an absorption schedule no filing supports.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The group has no bank debt: total liabilities of USD 43.12m at 30 September 2026 are trade payables, accruals, contract liabilities, taxes and an employment-benefit obligation, and the only borrowing-like item is USD 0.16m of lease liabilities [S4]. Finance costs of USD 0.04m in nine months are lease interest. Held at 8% on a negligible balance.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income was USD 0.27m in the nine months to September 2026 on an opening cash balance of USD 10.04m and a closing one of USD 20.86m [S4], about 2.5% on the average; the balance is mostly rupiah and dollar deposits. We use 2.5% rather than the 1.7% historical ratio, which was depressed by a lower average balance.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No borrowing plan is disclosed and the group is net cash; the September 2026 balance sheet carries no bank debt [S4]. Zero in every year.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The reported profits are flattered by non-operating items that should not be forecast: nine months of 2026 booked a USD 1.29m fair-value gain on listed equity securities, USD 0.35m of foreign-exchange gains and USD 2.61m of other gains against an operating result of about USD 0.15m after SG&A [S4, F18]. They are excluded rather than repeated; the gain on the listed portfolio is captured in net debt because the shares sit inside the pack's cash line [S4, F19].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The only subsidiary carries negative net liabilities of USD 3,578 at 30 September 2026 and no profit for the period [S4]; held at zero.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid in the price history the pack carries (dps zero in FY2022A-FY2025A) [S0], and the annual general meeting of 2 June 2026 resolved not to distribute a dividend for FY2025 because the year was a loss [S9]. The balance sheet carries USD 154.2m of unappropriated accumulated losses [S4, F17], so there is no distributable reserve to pay a cash dividend from and the base pays nothing; the legal route to a distribution (a deficit reduction or capital reduction, then a dividend, or a buyback) is a governance event we discuss in the report rather than model, because no filing or resolution announces one [S9].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 3,889,179,559 shares issued and no corporate action in the pack or in the 2026 annual meeting resolutions [S0, S9]. The public holds 14.51% of the shares [S2, F29], above the exchange's free-float floor, so there is no dilution or index event in the base case; the thin float is handled as a liquidity discount on the target, not as a share-count change.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for a US dollar reporting currency, 2.0%, which is also the cap the constitution sets for a USD reporter. Indonesian petrochemical demand grows faster, but a single-site converter with a 2.4% gross margin, a 14.5% public float and a supplier that controls the cost base should not be given a growth premium in perpetuity.

challenges.answer: The challenge is right and the model was internally inconsistent. FY2026E gross margin is now 1.78% before the cost link (effective 1.58%), calibrated so that nine months booked plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate reproduces the printed arithmetic: USD 3.760m at nine months plus a Q4 at the Q3 rate of negative USD 0.745m a quarter gives USD 3.010m of gross profit on USD 190.7m of revenue, a 1.58% margin [S3, S4, F10, F38]. FY2026E EBIT is now negative USD 1.85m and net profit negative USD 1.42m; the report no longer describes the company as at operating breakeven and says the FY2026E operating result is a small loss. We did not assume a Q4 recovery: the Q3 LK signed 29 October 2026 discloses nothing that supports one [S4].

The 20% figure was in the basis text and not in the input, and the input is what the engine uses. We keep 5% and rewrote the basis to derive it: raw materials are 83% of cost of goods sold and Ecogreen's palm-derived feedstock is 61% of COGS, which keys off the palm complex rather than crude [S4, F11, F12]; the non-Ecogreen raw material is 22% of COGS and only the glycol train, running at a fifth of nameplate, consumes the ethylene-linked portion, which is why 5% not 20% is the Brent-exposed share [S2, F21]. With 90% pass-through the net exposure is 0.5% of COGS, and the house Brent path from 96.0 in FY2026E to 84.0 in FY2027E moves gross profit by about 0.07% of COGS, roughly three per cent of modelled gross profit. The report now states that effect instead of the old 2%-of-COGS claim. The 2026 evidence supports a small number: raw materials rose 35.1% while revenue rose 32.5% and the margin still improved, so pass-through is close to complete [S4, F9, F11].

We could not source a breach, so the claim is withdrawn everywhere it appeared: §3, §5, §6, §7 and the share_change and terminal_growth bases. The annual report's share register is now the only ownership source: the three holders above five per cent hold 85.4916% between them and the general public holds 14.5084% [S2, F29, F37], which is above the exchange's free-float floor. The report states that the registry mirror in the data pack is internally inconsistent, with its own rows not adding to a hundred per cent, and that we use the register. The liquidity finding survives on a sourced basis: the float is thin and turnover is low, so the house liquidity discount still applies [S0]. The F29 fact was added from S2 p.62 with the verbatim quote.

Both narratives were rewritten to the shocks actually applied, and the shocks were reset to the values the text claims. Bear: revenue growth minus 0.04 in every year and gross margin minus 0.013, which puts the effective spread at about 1.1%, the level the audited accounts printed in FY2024 and FY2025 (0.94% and 1.13%) [S5, F2, F4], and the narrative now says the third-quarter gross loss becomes the run-rate rather than claiming a trough below the actuals. Bull: revenue growth plus 0.04 and gross margin plus 0.013, an effective spread of about 3.7%, which the narrative now describes as about a point above base and below the second-quarter 2026 spike, not as a hold at the Q2 level [S4]. The shocks are symmetric, the probabilities are 0.25/0.50/0.25, and §5 states all three scenario values from the engine rather than the old weighted number.

The site now has a value and it is in the bridge. S5 p.221 discloses 853,205 square metres of land under building rights across Merak, Karawang and Tangerang, carried at USD 65.08m of cost and not depreciated [S5, F30, F31]. We value the option as the land at its own carrying cost less the operating enterprise value given up if the site is sold, which is the only defensible number in the absence of a market comparable for a Banten coastal chemical site: USD 65.08m less the engine's EV of about USD 10.2m, carried at the 0.25 bull probability [S5]. The net USD 54.8m item is now the largest single bridge entry and is what turns the rating. We do not claim a replacement-cost or scrap value for the two trains because no filing discloses one and an integrated ethylene oxide unit is worth more running than scrapped; the land cost is the floor we can source. §4 carries both the area and the cost with the probability in the bridge table.

The paragraph has been rebuilt on the card's own measures. Accruals ratio is (net profit less operating cash flow) over average total assets: the FY2025 net loss against CFO of USD 3.17m on total assets of USD 152.56m [S5, F33, F34] gives a negative ratio, which is the conservative direction, and the report now says so instead of substituting FCFF. The capex claim is withdrawn: capex is an investing outflow and never enters operating cash flow, so the gap between capex and depreciation cannot explain CFO, and the report says that explicitly. The 9M2026 CFO of USD 10.13m is decomposed: inventories fell from USD 24.37m to USD 17.66m, a release of about USD 6.7m, plus a tax restitution and a payables increase [S4, F39, F40]. The receivables spike is quantified: USD 26.88m at 30 June against USD 10.51m at 31 December 2025, a 156% increase on 35% revenue growth, which trips the 1.5x divergence flag, and the report says so and then notes the unwind to USD 16.41m at 30 September [S3, S4, F35, F41, F42].

The 22% ramp had no source and is gone. The LK pays USD 0.18m of tax on nine-month pre-tax profit of USD 4.63m, a measured 3.9% rate, and booked a net benefit in FY2025 [S4, S5], and the group carries USD 154.2m of unappropriated accumulated losses against pre-tax profit of about one million a year, most of it interest on cash [S4, F17]. At that arithmetic the shield is not absorbed in four years; it is not absorbed in the forecast at all. We now hold 4%, the measured rate, through FY2030E and in the terminal year, and the basis states that the paid rate is already the after-shield rate rather than a precursor to a ramp. The MOST_LIKELY card's rule (use the rate the LK shows being paid) is followed literally.

The step is now dated by the filing's own depreciation arithmetic rather than by the fifth forecast year. At 31 December 2025 net property, plant and equipment was USD 92.79m, of which USD 65.08m was land at cost and never depreciated, leaving a depreciable base of about USD 27.7m against a FY2025 depreciation charge of USD 4.117m [S5, F31, F36, F7]: an average remaining depreciable life of about seven years, with machinery at a similar multiple of its own charge. Capex therefore ramps from 0.4% of revenue to 1.0% in FY2029E and 1.8% in FY2030E and settles at the depreciation rate from FY2031E, which is when that remaining life expires. The terminal rate is now the D&A rate (2.16%) rather than an arbitrary 2.3%, so FCFF in the tail is positive rather than negative and the terminal value is no longer a negative number; the report states that a shorter life takes the explicit value down and a longer one takes it up, and that the date is read from the accounts. The remaining uncertainty is the age of the individual units, which no filing discloses at that granularity.

The par mark was the most generous input in the valuation and it is now discounted. The portfolio is USD 8.87m of listed shares in five affiliated small caps the same group controls, at quoted prices, and a company with a 14.5% public float cannot realise those marks at size; a 20% liquidity and related-party discount is applied and the resulting negative item of USD 1.77m is a bridge entry at probability one, so it reduces every scenario including the bear [S4, F19, F29]. The 2026 mark-to-market gain of USD 1.29m is already inside the carrying value, so the discount is about realisability and not about a stale mark [S4, F20]; the report says that. The shares remain inside net cash rather than moved into a separate line, which is why the haircut is a bridge item and not a reclassification.

§2 now states both house paths with deck placeholders and reconciles them. Brent runs from spot to 96.0 in FY2026E to 84.0 in FY2027E; the CPO series the palm feedstock actually keys off runs from the FY2025A level to 1,135 in FY2026E and 1,240 in FY2027E, i.e. the two series point in opposite directions [S4]. That is why FY2027E revenue grows 4.0% while Brent falls: the palm-linked 61% of COGS is rising, the Brent-linked 5% is falling, and on a 90% pass-through the net effect of the Brent path is about 0.07% of COGS. The report states the split and says plainly that the oil deck is not the driver.

The citation was wrong and the legal view is now stated as law rather than as a filing fact. With USD 154.2m of unappropriated accumulated losses there is no distributable profit from which a cash dividend can be paid: Indonesian company law allows a distribution only out of positive retained earnings, and the shareholders in general meeting decide the appropriation [S4, F17, S9]. The deficit can only be absorbed by future profits, which at the modelled earning rate would take decades, or by a deficit or capital reduction approved by shareholders, which carries creditor-notice and solvency requirements; no filing or resolution announces either [S9]. We have added that route to the bull narrative, which now has the listed portfolio realised with the proceeds available to minorities, and we state in §6 that a buyback below book or a distribution after a deficit reduction is the route by which the cash could reach minorities. We deliberately do not add a cash-return shock to the bull case: the cash is already counted at face in net cash, so a distribution moves value only by closing the holding-company discount, and modelling a corporate action nobody has announced is how a base case stops being the most likely path.

Both are now sized and the ratings are corrected. flags.justification: The valuation weights use only DCF (dcf_fcff 1.0). Multiples are unusable for a business whose operating profit is about USD 0.2m: nine-month 2026 net profit of USD 4.45m rests on USD 4.25m of fair-value, FX and other gains below the operating line [S4, F18], so a price-earnings multiple would value non-operating items, and LTM EBITDA after restated depreciation is almost entirely the depreciation charge, making EV/EBITDA a multiple of an accounting entry. A price-to-book cross-check at book equity of USD 117.1m [S4] would value the company at several times the market price, because the book is a glycol plant running at a fifth of nameplate in an industry the government describes as oversupplied [S10]; we give it zero weight. The DCF alone captures the going-concern cash flow.
